stem: A company runs application servers in private subnets in three Availability Zones of one VPC. The servers reach the internet through one NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone. The company wants the servers in the other Availability Zones to keep internet access when one Availability Zone fails. Which solution is the MOST resilient?

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own Availability Zone.
options.why: Each zone then has its own NAT gateway, so a failure of one Availability Zone leaves the other zones with internet access.

options.text: Keep the one NAT gateway and add a second Elastic IP address to it so that it serves the three Availability Zones.
options.why: A second address does not move the gateway: the NAT gateway still lives in [a specific Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-az-scope).
options.misconception: believes that more addresses make a NAT gateway span zones

options.text: Create two more NAT gateways in the first Availability Zone and spread the routes of the private subnets across the three gateways.
options.why: The three gateways share one zone, because each NAT gateway is created in [a specific Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-az-scope), so one failure stops them together.
options.misconception: confuses more gateways with more Availability Zones

options.text: Attach a security group to the NAT gateway that allows traffic from the private subnets in the three Availability Zones.
options.why: You [cannot associate a security group](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-no-security-group) with a NAT gateway, and a security group adds no resilience.
options.misconception: treats a NAT gateway as an instance with a security group

explanation: The NAT gateway is the weak point, because each NAT gateway is created in [a specific Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-az-scope). When that zone fails, the servers in the other zones lose internet access. A NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, with routes that stay inside the zone, removes this dependency.
takeaway: For resilient outbound internet access, create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone.
twin: If the stem said "the LOWEST cost" instead: keep the one NAT gateway, because the requirement for resilience is gone and fewer gateways cost less.

stem: A company sends traffic from private subnets to the internet through one NAT gateway. A network engineer expects a peak of 60 Gbps next quarter and asks whether the company needs to replace the NAT gateway before the peak. What should a solutions architect answer?

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway before the peak, because its bandwidth stops at the starting value.
options.why: The [5 Gbps](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-bandwidth) value is where a NAT gateway starts, and it scales [up to 100 Gbps](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-bandwidth).
options.misconception: takes the starting bandwidth for the maximum

options.text: Keep the NAT gateway, because it scales to the expected bandwidth automatically.
options.why: A NAT gateway automatically scales [up to 100 Gbps](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-bandwidth), which is more than the expected peak.

options.text: Associate a larger security group with the NAT gateway to raise its bandwidth.
options.why: You [cannot associate a security group](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-no-security-group) with a NAT gateway, and a security group does not change bandwidth.
options.misconception: treats a security group as a size setting

options.text: Request a higher quota for NAT gateways per Availability Zone to raise the bandwidth.
options.why: The quota of [5 NAT gateways per Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-per-az-quota) counts gateways; it does not change the bandwidth of a gateway.
options.misconception: confuses a count quota with bandwidth

explanation: The expected peak is below the maximum of a NAT gateway: a NAT gateway supports [5 Gbps](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-bandwidth) of bandwidth and automatically scales [up to 100 Gbps](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-bandwidth). The company keeps the NAT gateway and changes nothing.
takeaway: A NAT gateway scales its bandwidth automatically, so check the peak against the maximum first.
twin: If the stem said "a peak of 150 Gbps" instead: split the resources into more subnets with a NAT gateway in each, because a gateway scales [up to 100 Gbps](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-bandwidth).
